subject: Internet of Things
stem: What are the address sizes of IPv4 and IPv6?
explanation: IPv4 uses 32-bit dotted-decimal addresses, which ran out; IPv6 uses 128 bits (2¹²⁸ addresses) in hexadecimal notation. 64 bits is the size of the IPv6 interface identifier, not the full address.
concept: IPv4 32-bit, IPv6 128-bit.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: What is an MQTT retained message?
options: The broker keeps every message forever for replay
A message the broker publishes when a client disconnects ungracefully
The broker stores the last retained message on a topic and sends it immediately to each new subscriber
A message the publisher resends until every subscriber acknowledges
explanation: A retained message lets a late-joining dashboard see the current state at once. Publishing on ungraceful disconnect is the Last Will and Testament, a different feature.
concept: Retained = last value per topic for new subscribers.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: Which description best defines the Internet of Things?
options: A global network of personal computers sharing files through web browsers
A single cloud server that stores spreadsheets uploaded by users
A network of physical objects with embedded sensors, software and connectivity that collect and exchange data
A wired telephone network that carries voice between exchanges
explanation: IoT means connected physical 'things' that sense, process and exchange data with other devices and systems. A network of personal computers is the ordinary Internet; what makes IoT distinct is the embedded sensing and actuation in physical objects.
concept: IoT = physical things + sensors/actuators + connectivity + data exchange.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: What is the difference between CoAP CON and NON messages?
options: CON uses TCP; NON uses UDP
CON is for responses only; NON is for requests only
CON must be acknowledged and is retransmitted if no ACK arrives; NON is not acknowledged
CON carries no payload; NON carries the payload
explanation: Confirmable messages give reliability over UDP through ACKs and exponential-backoff retransmission. Both types run over UDP, so the TCP/UDP split is wrong.
concept: CON = reliable (ACK + retransmit); NON = fire-and-forget.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: What happens under 1-persistent CSMA when several stations are waiting for a busy channel to clear?
options: They each wait a random time, so collisions are rare
They all transmit the moment the channel goes idle, so they collide
Only the station with the lowest address transmits
explanation: 1-persistent stations keep sensing and send immediately on idle, which is good at light load but guarantees a collision when two or more are waiting. Transmitting with probability 1/k is p-persistent behaviour.
concept: 1-persistent: optimistic; all waiters collide.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: In pure ALOHA, how does a sender learn that its frame collided, and what does it do next?
options: It senses the carrier during transmission and aborts immediately
The receiver sends a NACK on the same channel at once
It receives no ACK before the timeout, then waits a random backoff and retransmits
It retransmits immediately in the next slot without waiting
explanation: ALOHA has no carrier sensing; a missing acknowledgement signals failure, and a random backoff avoids a repeat collision. Immediate retransmission would make the same colliding pair collide again.
concept: ALOHA: transmit, wait for ACK, random backoff on timeout.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: As offered load G rises beyond the optimum on a contention MAC, what happens to useful throughput?
options: It falls, because collisions, backoffs and retransmissions grow
It keeps rising linearly with G
It stays fixed at the peak value
It rises only if packets are made shorter
explanation: Throughput curves such as G·e^(−G) are non-monotonic: past the peak, extra traffic mostly creates collisions and wasted energy. Assuming more traffic means more throughput is the trap.
concept: More offered traffic ≠ more throughput beyond the peak.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: Why do broadcast links need a medium access control (MAC) protocol?
options: Broadcast links have very high bit error rates over long distances
The medium is shared, so only one station can transmit successfully at a time
Each station has a dedicated wire to the receiver
Routing tables must be exchanged between stations
explanation: Simultaneous transmissions on a shared channel collide, so MAC decides how and when a node may start. High bit error rates over long distances describe point-to-point WAN links, where the concern is error control rather than access.
concept: Shared medium → collisions → MAC needed.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: Which set of functions belongs to an IoT edge gateway?
options: Aggregating field data, edge processing, protocol conversion and buffering
Generating the physical stimulus that sensors measure
Assigning radio frequencies to every node in the world
Replacing the cloud platform's long-term database
explanation: The gateway sits between local device networks and the cloud, aggregating, filtering, translating protocols and buffering during outages. Long-term storage at scale is the platform's job; a gateway only buffers temporarily.
concept: Gateway: aggregate, pre-process, translate protocols, buffer.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: Why is an LDR normally connected in a voltage divider before a microcontroller reads it?
options: An ADC measures voltage, so the resistance change must be converted into a proportional voltage
The divider increases the LDR's sensitivity to light
The divider converts light directly into digital codes
The divider protects the LDR from moisture
explanation: Microcontroller ADCs read voltages, not resistances; the divider turns R_LDR into Vout = Vin·R2/(R_LDR + R2). The divider does not change the LDR's intrinsic sensitivity and does not digitise anything; the ADC does that.
concept: Voltage divider turns resistance change into a readable voltage.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: Which pair of properties gives RFID its main operational advantage over barcodes in a warehouse?
options: Lower unit cost per label, and no reader is required
Data is printed permanently, so it cannot be rewritten
No line of sight is needed, and many tags can be read at once
Shorter read range, which prevents accidental reads
explanation: RFID reads through packaging and reads hundreds of tags concurrently, whereas barcodes need optical alignment and are scanned one at a time. Lower unit cost is a barcode advantage, not an RFID one, and RFID always needs an interrogator.
concept: RFID: no line of sight, bulk reads, rewritable, longer range; barcode: cheaper.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: Which transport and default ports does MQTT use?
explanation: MQTT runs over TCP on 1883, or 8883 when secured with TLS. UDP 5683/5684 are CoAP's ports.
concept: MQTT: TCP 1883 / TLS 8883.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: 500 remote sensors on a satellite link each send 1 reading per minute to 3 operator apps. How many satellite-link transmissions per hour occur with direct sending versus a broker in the cloud?
options: 30,000 direct versus 90,000 via a cloud broker
1,500 direct versus 500 via a cloud broker
90,000 direct versus 30,000 via a cloud broker
explanation: Direct: 500 × 3 × 60 = 90,000 over the satellite; with the broker in the cloud, each reading crosses the satellite once (30,000/h) and fan-out happens on terrestrial links. 90,000 in both cases ignores where the fan-out happens.
concept: Place the broker so fan-out avoids the expensive link.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: A publisher sends at QoS 2, and the subscriber subscribed at QoS 1. With no losses, how many MQTT control packets cross both hops for one message, and are duplicates possible at the subscriber?
explanation: Publisher→broker at QoS 2 uses 4 packets (PUBLISH/PUBREC/PUBREL/PUBCOMP); broker→subscriber runs at min(2,1) = QoS 1, using 2 packets, so 6 in total, and QoS 1 allows duplicates. 8 packets assumes QoS 2 end to end, ignoring the min rule.
concept: Effective QoS per hop = min(pub, sub).

subject: Internet of Things
stem: An LM35 (10 mV/°C) reads 25 °C into a 10-bit ADC with V_ref = 5 V. Using ADC = (V_in/V_ref)·(2ⁿ − 1) and rounding to the nearest integer, what code is reported?
explanation: V_in = 0.25 V, so 0.25/5 × 1023 = 51.15, which rounds to 51. Using 250 treats the millivolt reading as the code, skipping the ADC scaling.
concept: ADC code = V_in/V_ref × (2ⁿ − 1).

subject: Internet of Things
stem: Non-persistent CSMA with T = 1 ms, τ = 0.1 ms and g = 1000 packets/s. Using S = Ū/(B̄ + Ī), what is the throughput? (Round to 3 decimal places.)
explanation: G = gT = 1 and a = 0.1, so S = e^(−0.1)/(1.2 + e^(−0.1)) = 0.9048/2.1048 = 0.430. 0.451 uses (1 + a) instead of (1 + 2a), dropping one τ from the busy period.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: Two slotted-ALOHA devices: p_B = 0.2. What p_A makes S_A exactly twice S_B? (Round to 3 decimal places.)
explanation: S_A = 2S_B ⇔ p_A(1 − p_B) = 2p_B(1 − p_A) ⇔ p_A = 2p_B/(1 + p_B) = 0.4/1.2 = 0.333. Simply doubling to 0.4 gives a ratio of 0.32/0.12 = 2.67, not 2.
concept: p_A = 2p_B/(1 + p_B) for a 2:1 throughput ratio.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: Slotted ALOHA is overloaded at G = 2. What are the throughput and the mean number of attempts per successful packet? (S to 3 dp, attempts to 2 dp.)
explanation: S = 2e^(−2) = 0.271, and attempts per success = 1/P_s = e^G = 7.39. 2.72 attempts is the value at the G = 1 optimum, not at G = 2.
concept: Mean attempts = 1/P_s = e^G (slotted).

subject: Internet of Things
stem: What is the minimum number of ADC bits needed for 0.1 °C resolution with an LM35 at V_ref = 5 V, using the 2ⁿ − 1 convention?
explanation: 0.1 °C is 1 mV, so 2ⁿ − 1 ≥ 5000; 2¹² − 1 = 4095 is too few and 2¹³ − 1 = 8191 suffices. 12 bits is the tempting near-miss but falls short of 5000 steps.
concept: Bits needed: 2ⁿ − 1 ≥ V_ref/(K·resolution).

subject: Internet of Things
stem: A gateway takes n = 400 channel-sensing samples; normal busy probability is 0.2. Using a 3σ rule with σ = √(p(1 − p)/n), above what measured busy fraction should it raise a jamming alarm?
explanation: σ = √(0.16/400) = 0.02, so the threshold is 0.2 + 3 × 0.02 = 0.26. 0.22 is only a 1σ threshold, which would raise many false alarms.
concept: Jamming alarm when p̂_b > p_b^normal + kσ.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: 127-byte frames are sent at 250 kbps through air (v = 3×10⁸ m/s). What is the maximum distance for a ≤ 0.05? (Round to the nearest km.)
explanation: T = 1016/250,000 = 4.064 ms, so τ ≤ 0.2032 ms and d ≤ 0.2032 ms × 3×10⁸ ≈ 61 km. 41 km uses the cable speed, but the link is through air.
concept: d_max = a·T·v.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: Under p-persistent CSMA, k = 3 stations wait for the channel. What is P(exactly one transmits) at p = 0.5 and at p = 1/3? (3 dp.)
explanation: P = kp(1 − p)^(k−1): 3(0.5)(0.25) = 0.375 and 3(1/3)(4/9) = 0.444, so p = 1/k is better. The last pair gives a single named station's chance, not the chance that any one station succeeds.
concept: p = 1/k maximises the single-transmitter probability.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: For the ALOHAnet frame of 640 payload bits, 32 header bits and 32 parity bits, what is the framing efficiency? (Round to 1 decimal place.)
explanation: η = 640/704 = 90.9%. 95.2% forgets the parity bits in the frame length.
concept: Framing efficiency = payload/total bits.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: A CoAP CON exchange is tried up to 5 times; each try fails if either the request or ACK is lost, each independently with probability 0.1. What is P(all tries fail)? (3 significant figures.)
explanation: Per-try failure = 1 − 0.9² = 0.19, so P_fail = 0.19⁵ = 2.48e-04. 1.00×10⁻⁵ uses 0.1 per try, forgetting that losing the ACK also fails the exchange.
concept: P_fail = [1 − (1 − p)²]^(MAX_RETRANSMIT+1).

subject: Internet of Things
stem: With a = 0.01, how many times longer is the pure-ALOHA vulnerable period than CSMA's vulnerable period?
explanation: Pure ALOHA's window is 2T and CSMA's is τ, so the ratio is 2T/τ = 2/a = 200. 100× compares T with τ, forgetting that pure ALOHA's window is two frame times.
concept: Vulnerable-window ratio = 2/a.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: Slotted ALOHA runs at G = 0.5 (P_s = e^(−0.5)); each attempt plus backoff takes 25 ms. What deadline D_max gives a miss probability ≤ 0.01?
explanation: P_s = 0.607, so m ≥ ln 0.01/ln 0.393 = 4.94 → 5 attempts, i.e. 125 ms. 100 ms allows only 4 attempts, giving P_miss = 0.024 > 0.01.
concept: Deadline = attempts needed × time per attempt.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: Under slotted ALOHA at G = 1, each attempt succeeds independently with P_s = e^(−1). What is the probability a packet needs exactly 3 attempts? (Round to 3 decimal places.)
explanation: Geometric: (1 − P_s)² × P_s = (0.632)² × 0.368 = 0.147. 0.253 is the probability of needing more than 3 attempts.
concept: Attempts are geometric with parameter P_s.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: A farm deploys 300 battery soil sensors over 12 km. Each sends one 50 ms uplink every 15 minutes over an LPWAN with uncoordinated, pure-ALOHA-like access. Which assessment is best supported? (Load to 3 dp, success to 2 dp.)
options: Inadequate: pure ALOHA collapses at any load above 0.017, so CSMA is mandatory
Use Wi-Fi mesh instead, because LPWAN cannot reach 12 km
Adequate: new load is about 0.017, far below the 0.184 peak, so P_s ≈ 0.97; no carrier sensing or slotting is needed
Inadequate: slotting is required because pure ALOHA cannot carry a load of 0.017
explanation: λT = (300/900) × 0.05 = 0.0167; solving G·e^(−2G) = 0.0167 gives G ≈ 0.0173, so P_s = e^(−2G) ≈ 0.97, far from the 0.184 peak at G = 0.5. Wi-Fi mesh is the tempting 'reliable' answer, but its short range and energy cost make it unsuitable for a 12 km battery deployment.
concept: Check offered load against S_max before adding MAC complexity.
source: Owner's IoT notes; scenario style inspired by Bahga & Madisetti, IoT: A Hands-On Approach

subject: Internet of Things
stem: A gateway takes 400 sensing samples per window; normal busy probability is 0.2, and it alarms when the measured busy fraction exceeds 0.2 + 3σ (σ = √(p(1 − p)/n)). A jammer turns a fraction j of otherwise-idle samples busy. What is the smallest detectable duty j?
explanation: Threshold = 0.26; the measured busy fraction becomes 0.2 + j × 0.8, so j ≥ 0.06/0.8 = 7.5%. 6.0% sets j equal to the threshold excess, forgetting that the jammer can only convert the 80% of samples that were idle.
concept: Low-duty jammers can hide below statistical thresholds.
source: Owner's IoT notes; scenario style inspired by Bahga & Madisetti, IoT: A Hands-On Approach

subject: Internet of Things
stem: An energy app must switch off a valve via MQTT. The team proposes QoS 2 for 'exactly-once' control. Which design best ensures the valve is actually closed once?
options: Send a command with a unique command ID, have the device act idempotently and publish its new state on a separate state topic, and confirm the state
Rely on QoS 2 alone, because exactly-once delivery means the valve closes exactly once
Use QoS 0 and publish the command three times to be safe
Publish the command and the state on the same topic so the device sees its own echo
explanation: QoS 2 only prevents duplicate delivery on each hop; it does not prove the actuator moved, so application-level IDs, idempotent handling and state confirmation are needed. Sharing one topic for command and state is tempting for simplicity but can make a device loop on its own echo.
concept: QoS ≠ actuation guarantee; separate command/state and confirm.
source: Owner's IoT notes; scenario style inspired by Bahga & Madisetti, IoT: A Hands-On Approach

subject: Internet of Things
stem: In a multi-hop smart-classroom sensor grid, which layer ensures end-to-end reliability between the far desk node and the destination?
explanation: The transport layer handles source-to-destination reliability across all hops. The network layer is tempting because it computes the multi-hop route, but routing a packet is not the same as guaranteeing its end-to-end delivery.
concept: Link: hop-by-hop; network: routing; transport: end-to-end.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: What is the main purpose of fog computing in an IoT pipeline?
options: Process, filter and translate data locally before long-haul transmission to the cloud
Encrypt sensor data at the transducer before conversion
Replace all wireless links with wired Ethernet
Store raw data permanently on each sensor node
explanation: Fog nodes reduce data, drop redundant readings and translate protocols (for example, Zigbee to MQTT) close to the devices, cutting latency and backhaul load. Encryption at the transducer is not fog computing; fog sits at the gateway or local-network tier.
concept: Fog = local processing between devices and cloud to cut latency and backhaul.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: In the four-layer IoT model, what is the correct bottom-to-top order?
explanation: Sensors and actuators (perception) feed connectivity (network), which feeds processing (middleware/cloud), which serves users (application). Putting middleware below the network is tempting but wrong, because data must be transported before a cloud or edge platform can process it.
concept: Four layers: perception, network, middleware/cloud, application.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: A new analytics app subscribes to sensor data without the sensors knowing its address. Which pub/sub decoupling is this?
explanation: Space decoupling means publishers and subscribers need no knowledge of each other's address or identity. Time decoupling is about not having to be online at the same moment.
concept: Pub/sub decouples space, time and synchronisation.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: When does an MQTT broker publish a client's Last Will and Testament (LWT)?
options: When the client drops out ungracefully, such as when its keep-alive expires
Whenever the client sends a clean DISCONNECT
Every time the client publishes a QoS 2 message
When a new subscriber joins the will topic
explanation: The will is registered at CONNECT and released only on an ungraceful drop, letting others learn the device is offline. A clean DISCONNECT discards the will, which is the tempting misconception.
concept: LWT fires on ungraceful disconnect only.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: What does a non-persistent CSMA station do when it senses the channel busy?
options: It keeps sensing continuously and sends as soon as the channel is idle
It waits a random time and then senses again
It sends with probability p in the next slot
explanation: Non-persistent CSMA backs off randomly, spreading waiting stations apart, which suits heavy load but wastes idle time at light load. Continuous sensing and immediate sending is 1-persistent behaviour.
concept: Non-persistent: busy → random wait → re-sense.

subject: Internet of Things
topic: IoT vs CPS vs digital twin
stem: A classroom system senses temperature and automatically switches the AC on above 27 °C and off below 24 °C. What turns this IoT system into a cyber-physical system?
options: The use of a cloud dashboard to display the temperature
The ability to predict the temperature ten minutes ahead
The closed feedback loop: sense → compute → actuate → physical response → sense
The use of Wi-Fi instead of Zigbee for connectivity
explanation: A CPS couples computation to physical actuation in a closed loop, so the measured state drives control action. Prediction of a future state is the domain of a digital twin, so it does not by itself make the system a CPS.
concept: CPS = sensing + computation + actuation in a closed loop.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: For a gas-leak alarm, why is average throughput an inadequate MAC performance metric?
options: Gas sensors send too few packets to measure throughput
Alarms are always sent over wired links
Average throughput already guarantees bounded delay
Packets must meet a deadline, P(D > D_max) ≤ ε; a late alarm is useless even if delivered intact
explanation: Safety-critical traffic needs bounded latency with a small violation probability ε, which averages cannot express. High average throughput can coexist with occasional long backoff chains that break the deadline.
concept: Mission-critical IoT: deadline-constrained reliability, not average throughput.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: What is the vulnerable period of a frame of duration T in pure ALOHA?
explanation: Any other start within T before or T after a frame's start overlaps it, giving a 2T window. T is the vulnerable period of slotted ALOHA, where starts are aligned to slot boundaries.
concept: Pure ALOHA vulnerable period = 2T; slotted = T.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: What is the scale factor of the LM35 temperature sensor?
options: 10 mV per K, offset by 273 mV
explanation: The LM35 outputs V = 0.01·T volts with T in °C, so 25 °C gives 0.25 V. A kelvin-based output with an offset describes a different sensor family, not the LM35.
concept: LM35: V_out = 10 mV/°C × T.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: Which description fits DDS?
options: An IETF REST protocol over UDP for constrained devices
An OMG standard for brokerless, data-centric pub/sub with typed topics and rich QoS
A cloud automation service linking web apps
A broker-based message-centric protocol over TCP
explanation: DDS peers discover each other (RTPS) and share typed, keyed data with 20+ QoS policies such as DEADLINE and RELIABILITY. A broker-based message-centric protocol over TCP is MQTT.
concept: DDS: OMG, brokerless, data-centric, rich QoS.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: Why is giving every node its own frequency (FDM) a poor fit for a local sensor network?
options: Nodes tuned to their own frequencies cannot hear each other's transmissions, yet the goal is mutual communication
FDM requires every node to have a wired connection
FDM causes more collisions than random access
FDM works only for optical links
explanation: FDM removes contention, but a receiver on its own band cannot receive what others send, which defeats a network where any node may talk to any other. Saying FDM causes more collisions is wrong; it causes none, which is why it looks attractive at first.
concept: Per-node frequencies stop collisions but also stop nodes hearing each other.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: For pure (unslotted) ALOHA with N = 10 nodes and S = Np(1 − p)^(2(N−1)), what is the exact optimal transmit probability p*? (Round to 4 decimal places.)
explanation: Setting d/dp[p(1 − p)^(2N−2)] = 0 gives p* = 1/(2N − 1) = 1/19. 1/(2N) = 0.05 is a common approximation that is close but not the maximiser.
concept: Pure finite-N: p* = 1/(2N − 1).

subject: Internet of Things
stem: An ADC reference drifts to 4.9 V, but firmware still assumes 5.0 V (10-bit, 2ⁿ − 1, rounding). The true temperature from an LM35 is 30 °C. What temperature is displayed? (Round to 2 decimal places.)
explanation: Code = 0.3/4.9 × 1023 = 62.63 → 63; firmware converts 63 × 5/1023 → 30.79 °C, so a low reference reads hot. 30.61 °C is the ratio-only estimate that skips the rounding of the code.
concept: Reference drift causes systematic gain error.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: A channel carries G = 100 attempts/s with P_s = 0.3. How many retransmissions per second does it carry?
explanation: Successes S = G·P_s = 30/s, so retransmissions G − S = 70/s. 30/s is the success rate, not the retransmission rate.
concept: Retransmission rate = G(1 − P_s).

subject: Internet of Things
stem: A node has a 10 kJ battery and sends 8,640 packets/day at 1 mJ each. What is its lifetime, and what if an attacker forces 10 retries per packet? (Whole days.)
explanation: Normal: 8.64 J/day gives 1157 days; with 10 retries each packet costs 11 transmissions (95.04 J/day), giving 105 days. Dividing by 10 forgets the original transmission in addition to the 10 retries.
concept: E_attack = n·E_retry drains batteries multiplicatively.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: p-persistent CSMA uses p = 0.5 (tuned for 2 waiters), but k = 5 stations are waiting. What is the probability of a collision in a round? (Round to 3 decimal places.)
explanation: P(idle) = 0.5⁵ = 0.031 and P(success) = 5(0.5)(0.5⁴) = 0.156, so P(collision) = 0.812. 0.969 is P(at least one transmits), which wrongly includes the successful rounds.
concept: Over-estimated p with many waiters → mostly collisions.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: Which topic matches the subscription filter home/+/temp?
explanation: + stands for exactly one level, so home/room1/temp matches. Home/room1/temp fails because topics are case-sensitive, and the others have the wrong number of levels.
concept: + = one level; topics are case-sensitive.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: 1000-bit frames travel through air (v = 3×10⁸ m/s) at 1 Mbps. At what distance does a reach 1?
explanation: T = 1 ms, so a = 1 when τ = 1 ms, i.e. d = 3×10⁸ × 10⁻³ = 300 km. 300 m is the answer at 1 Gbps, where T is 1 µs.
concept: a = 1 when d = v·T.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: A 10-bit ADC (V_ref = 5 V, 2ⁿ − 1 convention) connected to an LM35 reads code 62. What temperature does it represent? (Round to 2 decimal places.)
explanation: V = 62 × 5/1023 = 0.3030 V, and dividing by 0.01 V/°C gives 30.30 °C. 30.27 °C uses 1024 instead of the stated 2ⁿ − 1 convention.
concept: T = code × V_ref/((2ⁿ − 1)·K).

subject: Internet of Things
stem: A slotted-ALOHA channel is measured to deliver S = 0.2. Which offered loads G are consistent with this? (Round to 3 significant figures.)
options: G ≈ 0.259 only; the other root is negative
explanation: G·e^(−G) = 0.2 has two positive roots, 0.259 and 2.54, either side of the peak at G = 1. Assuming G = S ignores the retransmissions that G counts.
concept: Each S < S_max has two G roots: stable and overloaded.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: 200 valves are polled with CoAP GET every 10 s (2 messages per poll), or watched with Observe using CON notifications (2 messages per change) at 6 changes per hour each. What are the messages per hour?
explanation: Polling: 200 × 360 polls × 2 = 144,000/h; Observe: 200 × 6 × 2 = 2,400/h. 72,000 and 1,200 forget the response/ACK, counting only one message per exchange.
concept: Observe beats polling when change rate < poll rate.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: 10,000 sensors each publish once per second, and every message has 20 subscribers. What are the publication rate and the broker's delivery rate?
explanation: R_pub = N·f = 10,000/s, and R_del = N·K·f = 20 × 10,000 = 200,000/s. 200,000 publications would be the device-side cost of direct communication, not pub/sub.
concept: R_pub = N·f; R_del = N·K·f.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: A broker can make 50,000 deliveries/s. 20,000 sensors publish; 60% of messages have 2 subscribers and 40% have 5. What is the maximum per-sensor publish rate? (Round to 2 decimal places.)
explanation: K̄ = 0.6 × 2 + 0.4 × 5 = 3.2, so f_max = 50,000/(20,000 × 3.2) = 0.78/s. 0.71 uses the unweighted mean of 2 and 5 instead of the traffic-weighted mean.
concept: Mixed fan-out: K̄ = Σwᵢ·Kᵢ; f_max = C/(N·K̄).

subject: Internet of Things
stem: The ALOHAnet channel sends one 29 ms frame at a time. At the slotted-ALOHA peak, how many useful frames per second get through? (Round to 1 decimal place.)
explanation: Capacity = 1/0.029 = 34.5 frames/s, and the slotted peak is 1/e, giving 12.7 frames/s. 6.3 frames/s is the pure-ALOHA peak of 1/(2e).
concept: Useful rate = capacity × S.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: At the same offered load G = 1, how do pure ALOHA, slotted ALOHA and non-persistent CSMA (a = 0.01) rank by throughput?
explanation: Pure: e^(−2) = 0.135; slotted: e^(−1) = 0.368; NP-CSMA: 0.493, since sensing shrinks the vulnerable window to τ. Treating all as 0.368 confuses slotted ALOHA's peak with the others' values at G = 1.
concept: Sensing beats slotting when a is small.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: A 500 m cable LAN (v = 2×10⁸ m/s) carries 1000-bit frames at 10 Mbps. What is a = τ/T?
explanation: τ = 500/2×10⁸ = 2.5 µs and T = 1000/10⁷ = 100 µs, so a = 0.025. 40 is T/τ, the inverse ratio.
concept: a = τ/T; τ = d/v, T = L/R.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: A long-range link has a = τ/T = 0.5. A designer must choose between non-persistent CSMA and slotted ALOHA for maximum throughput. Which choice is justified? (3 dp.)
options: Slotted ALOHA: its peak 0.368 exceeds NP-CSMA's peak of about 0.236 at a = 0.5
NP-CSMA: carrier sensing always beats ALOHA, so its peak exceeds 0.368
Either: both peak at 0.5 regardless of a
NP-CSMA: at a = 0.5 its peak reaches about 0.815
explanation: Maximising S = G·e^(−aG)/[G(1 + 2a) + e^(−aG)] at a = 0.5 gives about 0.236 at G ≈ 0.82, below slotted ALOHA's 1/e. 0.815 is NP-CSMA's peak at a = 0.01; sensing only pays off when propagation is small relative to frame time.
concept: CSMA's advantage vanishes as a grows.
source: Owner's IoT notes; scenario style inspired by Bahga & Madisetti, IoT: A Hands-On Approach

subject: Internet of Things
stem: A campus needs location-wise views (everything in a room) and function-wise access control (only the energy department may command lights). Which topic design best fits?
options: One flat topic campus/data carrying a JSON 'type' field that the ACL filters on
A location-first hierarchy with the energy app granted read/write on campus/#
A functional namespace such as campus/energy/light/<bldg>/<floor>/<room>/state and …/command, with the energy app's ACL on campus/energy/#
Mirror every message into both hierarchies, which costs the broker nothing extra
explanation: A function-first subtree gives clean least-privilege ACLs, and separate state/command topics prevent echo loops; room views are still possible with + at the function levels. Mirroring is workable but doubles R_pub and the topic count, so 'costs nothing extra' is false.
concept: Design the hierarchy around who needs access, and split state from command.
source: Owner's IoT notes; scenario style inspired by Bahga & Madisetti, IoT: A Hands-On Approach

subject: Internet of Things
stem: A compromised sensor with valid credentials publishes fake 90 °C readings over TLS to its authorised topic. Which control would actually detect or limit this?
options: Per-device payload signing plus subscriber-side plausibility checks against neighbouring sensors
Tightening the ACL on the sensor's own topic
explanation: TLS and ACLs already pass because the device is authenticated and authorised, and the broker cannot judge data truth, so integrity and plausibility must be checked end to end. Tightening the ACL is tempting, but the sensor legitimately needs write access to that topic.
concept: Authenticated ≠ truthful: add data-level integrity and anomaly checks.
source: Owner's IoT notes; scenario style inspired by Bahga & Madisetti, IoT: A Hands-On Approach

subject: Internet of Things
stem: What is a keyed instance in DDS?
options: A topic that requires a password key to subscribe
Samples sharing the same key value (for example robot_id) are treated as one instance of a topic
A message encrypted with a session key
The broker's index of retained messages
explanation: Keys let many writers share one typed topic while readers track per-instance state and history. Encryption keys are a security mechanism and unrelated to DDS instance keys.
concept: DDS key field identifies instances within a topic.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: What are the maximum throughput of slotted ALOHA and the offered load at which it occurs?
explanation: S = G·e^(−G) peaks where dS/dG = 0, at G = 1, giving 1/e. The 0.184 at G = 0.5 is the pure-ALOHA peak, which has a doubled vulnerable period.
concept: Slotted ALOHA: S_max = 1/e at G = 1.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: What is a key weakness of token-based (contention-free) MAC in dynamic IoT deployments?
options: A node failure can lose the token, and joining nodes need explicit ring reconfiguration
Collisions occur every time two nodes hold data
Nodes must sense the carrier before every transmission
explanation: Token schemes keep a synchronised logical ring; a failed node drops the token and halts traffic until recovery, and new nodes cannot join automatically. Collisions are the weakness of contention schemes, which tokens avoid.
concept: Token MAC: no collisions, but fragile under joins and failures.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: In p-persistent CSMA with k stations waiting, what value of p maximises the chance that exactly one transmits?
explanation: kp(1 − p)^(k−1) is maximised at p = 1/k, the same result as finite-N slotted ALOHA. p = 1 is 1-persistent, which guarantees a collision when k ≥ 2.
concept: p-persistent optimum: p ≈ 1/(number of waiters).

subject: Internet of Things
stem: How does a continuous jammer exploit CSMA's politeness?
options: It forces nodes to transmit at higher power
Legitimate nodes keep sensing the channel busy and defer indefinitely
It decrypts frames by listening to the carrier
It makes the channel appear idle so nodes collide
explanation: CSMA nodes defer when the medium is busy, so a jammer that keeps it busy drives P_success to 0 and delay towards infinity while draining batteries. Making the channel look idle is the opposite of what a continuous jammer does.
concept: Jamming turns CSMA deferral into denial of service.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: What does the MQTT wildcard + match?
options: Any single character within a level
explanation: + substitutes for exactly one level between slashes, so home/+/temp matches home/room1/temp but not home/r1/a/temp. Zero or more levels is the behaviour of #.
concept: + = exactly one level.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: A client subscribes to home/# on a broker with ACLs enabled. What decides which messages it actually receives?
options: The filter alone; # always grants access to the whole subtree
The broker's ACL read permissions; a subscription filter is not a permission
The order in which clients connected
explanation: The broker matches filters and then checks the ACL, so a wide filter only reaches topics the user may read. Treating the filter as an access grant is a frequent security mistake.
concept: Filter ≠ permission; ACL decides.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: For a 10-bit ADC, how many output levels exist and what is the largest code?
explanation: n bits give 2ⁿ = 1024 distinct codes numbered 0 to 1023. Saying there are 1023 levels confuses the count of levels with the maximum code value.
concept: n-bit ADC: 2ⁿ levels, codes 0 … 2ⁿ − 1.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: The term 'Internet of Things' was coined in 1999 while solving which practical problem?
options: Routing packets between incompatible university networks
Sharing a radio channel among terminals on several islands
Tracking goods through a supply chain with RFID tags instead of manual barcode scans
Controlling factory robots with real-time middleware
explanation: The term came from a consumer-goods supply-chain project that used RFID to track inventory automatically. Interconnecting incompatible networks was the problem the Internet Protocol solved decades earlier, not the origin of the IoT term.
concept: IoT term originated in RFID-based supply-chain tracking (1999).

subject: Internet of Things
stem: In a sensor's three functional stages, which stage converts the detected physical change into an electrical quantity?
explanation: Transduction changes energy domain, producing a change in resistance, capacitance, voltage or current. Detection is the sensing element registering the stimulus, and signal conditioning only refines a signal that already exists.
concept: Sensor stages: detection → transduction → signal conditioning.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: Which three technologies are LPWAN (low-power wide-area) standards?
explanation: LPWANs trade data rate for kilometre-scale range on very little power. Wi-Fi, Zigbee and Z-Wave are local-area technologies with ranges of tens of metres.
concept: LPWAN: LoRaWAN, Sigfox, NB-IoT.

subject: Internet of Things
topic: IoT vs CPS vs digital twin
stem: Which question can a digital twin answer that neither a basic IoT server nor a threshold-based CPS can?
options: What is the current room temperature?
What will the room temperature be in ten minutes if the AC is switched on now?
Should the AC be on, given the temperature is above the threshold?
Which sensor sent the latest reading?
explanation: A digital twin keeps a computational model of the asset, so it can predict future states and evaluate alternative actions. Deciding whether the AC should be on at a threshold is what a CPS already does without any predictive model.
concept: Digital twin = model of the asset that predicts and evaluates what-if actions.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: On a QoS 1 hop, PUBLISH and PUBACK are each lost independently with probability 0.1, and the sender retransmits until it gets a PUBACK. What is the expected number of duplicate deliveries per message? (Round to 3 decimal places.)
explanation: Each attempt delivers with probability 0.9 and completes with 0.81, so E[deliveries] = 0.9/0.81 = 1.111 and E[duplicates] = 0.111. 0.235 is the expected number of extra PUBLISH transmissions, which includes attempts that never arrived.
concept: QoS 1 duplicates = p/(1 − p) when PUBACKs are lost.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: 500 sensors each publish once per interval to K = 4 subscribers. Comparing pub/sub with direct sensor-to-app sending, which statement is correct?
options: Pub/sub carries 500 messages in total versus 2,000 direct
Both carry exactly 2,000 messages in total
Pub/sub carries 2,000 messages in total, all from the sensors
Pub/sub carries 2,500 messages in total versus 2,000 direct, but sensor sends fall from 2,000 to 500
explanation: Pub/sub sends N = 500 up plus N·K = 2,000 down, giving N(1 + K) = 2,500, while direct sending is N·K = 2,000. Saying pub/sub carries only 500 counts the uplink and ignores the broker's fan-out.
concept: Pub/sub cuts sensor sends, not total traffic.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: Stations send 1000-bit frames at 100 kbps under pure ALOHA, each generating 1 frame/s. What is the maximum number of stations at the throughput peak? (Largest whole number.)
explanation: Capacity is 100 frames/s, and the pure peak 0.184 × 100 = 18.4 frames/s, so 18 stations fit. 36 uses the slotted peak of 0.368.
concept: N_max = S_max × capacity / per-station rate.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: For non-persistent CSMA with a = 0.01, what happens to S when G increases from 10 to 100? (3 dp.)
explanation: S(10) = 0.815 is near the peak, but at G = 100, aG = 1 and S = 0.359, so throughput collapses. 0.990 uses the a → 0 limit, which never turns down.
concept: NP-CSMA is non-monotonic once aG is large.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: A ground–GEO-satellite–ground path is 72,000 km (v = 3×10⁸ m/s) and frames take 29 ms. What is a, and what does it imply? (a to 1 decimal place.)
options: a ≈ 8.3; sensed state is stale, so CSMA behaves like ALOHA
explanation: τ = 0.24 s, so a = 0.24/0.029 ≈ 8.3. With a ≫ 1, a node cannot know whether others have started, so CSMA loses its advantage; claiming CSMA still wins ignores that sensing information is out of date.
concept: a ≫ 1 → carrier sensing is useless.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: A 2048-byte message is split into ALOHAnet packets with 80-character (640-bit) payloads and 704-bit total length. How many packets and total bits are needed?
explanation: 2048 × 8 = 16,384 bits ÷ 640 = 25.6, which rounds up to 26 packets, and 26 × 704 = 18,304 bits. 25 packets truncates the fraction and loses the last partial payload.
concept: Segment with ceiling; count overhead per packet.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: Which of these MQTT subscription filters is invalid?
explanation: # must be the last character of a filter, so a/#/c is malformed. +/+/c is valid because + may appear at any level, including the first.
concept: # must be last; + may appear anywhere.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: Under p-persistent CSMA with k = 3 waiters and p = 1/3, each round independently yields a success with probability 4/9. What is the expected number of rounds until the first success? (Round to 2 decimal places.)
explanation: Rounds are geometric, so the mean is 1/(4/9) = 2.25. 3.00 assumes one round per station, which ignores that idle and collided rounds simply repeat.
concept: Mean rounds = 1/P(success).

subject: Internet of Things
stem: Slotted ALOHA nodes use p = 0.1 (tuned for N = 10), but N = 20 nodes are active. What is the throughput, and how does it compare with the optimum for N = 20? (3 dp.)
explanation: S = 20 × 0.1 × 0.9¹⁹ = 0.270, while p = 1/20 would give 0.95¹⁹ = 0.377, so mis-tuning costs about 28%. Assuming throughput is unchanged ignores that more nodes at the same p collide more.
concept: p must track N; stale p collapses throughput.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: Non-persistent CSMA has S = G·e^(−aG)/[G(1 + 2a) + e^(−aG)]. What is S at G = 1 and a = 0.01? (Round to 3 decimal places.)
explanation: Numerator e^(−0.01) = 0.990; denominator 1.02 + 0.990 = 2.010; S = 0.493. 0.500 is the a → 0 limit G/(1 + G), which ignores the small propagation penalty.
concept: NP-CSMA throughput formula with G = gT, a = τ/T.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: CoAP's first header byte is Ver(2 bits) | Type(2 bits: CON 0, NON 1, ACK 2, RST 3) | TKL(4 bits), with Ver = 1; the Code byte = class × 32 + detail. What are the first byte for a CON with a 2-byte token, and the code byte for 2.05 Content?
explanation: 01 00 0010 = 0x42, and 2 × 32 + 5 = 69 = 0x45. 0x52 encodes Type = 1, which is NON, not CON.
concept: CoAP header bit layout and code encoding.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: Slotted ALOHA has N = 4 nodes, each transmitting with p = 0.25 per slot. What is the throughput? (Round to 3 decimal places.)
explanation: S = Np(1 − p)^(N−1) = 4 × 0.25 × 0.75³ = 0.422. 0.105 is one node's success probability, not the channel total.
concept: Finite-N slotted: S = Np(1 − p)^(N−1).

subject: Internet of Things
stem: What is the temperature resolution (°C per count) of an LM35 on a 10-bit ADC with V_ref = 5 V, using the 2ⁿ − 1 convention? (Round to 3 decimal places.)
explanation: 1 LSB = 5/1023 = 4.888 mV, and 4.888 mV ÷ 10 mV/°C = 0.489 °C. 4.888 is the step in millivolts, not converted to °C.
concept: Resolution in °C = (V_ref/(2ⁿ − 1))/K.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: An LDR is in series with R2 = 10 kΩ across 5 V, and V_out is taken across R2. What is V_out in bright light when R_LDR = 1 kΩ? (Round to 3 decimal places.)
explanation: V_out = 5 × 10/(1 + 10) = 4.545 V. 0.455 V is the drop across the LDR rather than across R2.
concept: V_out = V_in·R2/(R_LDR + R2).

subject: Internet of Things
stem: Each sensor sends a 20 ms packet every 10 s on a slotted-ALOHA channel. What is the largest whole number of sensors whose new traffic does not exceed the slotted peak 1/e?
explanation: Per-sensor load = 0.02/10 = 0.002, and (1/e)/0.002 = 183.94, so 183 sensors. 91 uses the pure-ALOHA peak 1/(2e).
concept: N_max = S_max × T_report/T_pkt.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: A swarm of 40 robots shares pose updates every 20 ms; any sample older than 50 ms is useless, and no single point of failure is allowed. Which middleware fits best?
options: MQTT with QoS 2 through one central broker
CoAP with each robot polling every other robot by GET
IFTTT applets triggered by each pose change
DDS with a typed, keyed topic (robot_id) and DEADLINE/RELIABILITY QoS over brokerless discovery
explanation: DDS offers deadline and freshness QoS, peer-to-peer discovery with no broker, and keyed instances per robot. MQTT QoS 2 is tempting for reliability, but it guarantees delivery only, not freshness, and its broker is a single point of failure.
concept: Real-time, brokerless, deadline-aware data → DDS.
source: Owner's IoT notes; scenario style inspired by Bahga & Madisetti, IoT: A Hands-On Approach

subject: Internet of Things
stem: A gas-leak alarm uses slotted ALOHA with 5 ms attempts and a fixed 20 ms backoff between attempts; the deadline is 60 ms and the miss probability must be ≤ 0.01. What is the largest offered load G that meets the requirement? (Round to 3 decimal places.)
explanation: 5m + 20(m − 1) ≤ 60 ⇒ m = 3 attempts; (1 − P_s)³ ≤ 0.01 needs P_s ≥ 0.785, so e^(−G) ≥ 0.785 ⇒ G ≤ 0.243. G = 1 maximises throughput but gives P_s = 0.368 and P_miss ≈ 0.25, far above 0.01.
concept: Deadline constraints cap load well below the throughput optimum.
source: Owner's IoT notes; scenario style inspired by Bahga & Madisetti, IoT: A Hands-On Approach

subject: Internet of Things
stem: Two slotted-ALOHA devices must keep p_A = 2p_B (A has priority). What choice maximises total throughput S_A + S_B, and what is the maximum?
explanation: Total = p_A(1 − p_B) + p_B(1 − p_A) = 3p_B − 4p_B²; setting the derivative to zero gives p_B = 3/8 and total 9/16. p_B = 1/3 is tempting as a 'balanced' choice but gives 0.5556, slightly below the optimum.
concept: Constrained optimisation of two-node slotted ALOHA.
source: Owner's IoT notes; scenario style inspired by Bahga & Madisetti, IoT: A Hands-On Approach

subject: Internet of Things
stem: What does the parameter a = τ/T capture, and which value is favourable for CSMA?
options: Frame time relative to propagation delay; a ≫ 1 is favourable
Offered load relative to capacity; a = 1 is favourable
Propagation delay relative to frame time; a ≪ 1 is favourable
Bit error rate relative to frame length; a = 0.5 is favourable
explanation: Small a means a sensed idle channel is truly idle, so CSMA's vulnerable window τ is tiny compared with T. When a ≥ 1, sensed information is stale and CSMA behaves like ALOHA.
concept: a = τ/T; small a → CSMA effective.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: Among Sigfox, LoRaWAN, NB-IoT and LTE-M, which offers the lowest data rate (about 0.1 kbps) but up to roughly 40 km range?
explanation: Sigfox is an ultra-narrowband operator network with very low data rate and the longest range in the comparison. LoRaWAN is the tempting choice, but it runs at 0.3–50 kbps with up to about 20 km.
concept: Sigfox: ~0.1 kbps, up to ~40 km.

subject: Internet of Things
topic: IoT vs CPS vs digital twin
stem: The statement 'The temperature is 27.7 °C' with no further action is characteristic of which kind of system?
explanation: Basic IoT senses and reports the current state without autonomous decisions. A CPS would add an action such as switching the AC on, so a bare reading is not CPS behaviour.
concept: IoT reports state; CPS controls; DT predicts.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: Which transport and architectural style does CoAP use?
options: Publish/subscribe over TCP through a broker
REST request/response over UDP (port 5683, 5684 with DTLS)
explanation: CoAP brings web-style GET/PUT/POST/DELETE to constrained devices over UDP. Broker-based pub/sub over TCP describes MQTT.
concept: CoAP: REST over UDP 5683/5684.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: With round-to-nearest quantisation, what is the maximum quantisation error of an ideal ADC?
options: Zero, because the code is rounded
explanation: Rounding to the nearest step means the true value can be at most half a step from the chosen code. ±1 LSB is the bound for truncation-style conversion, not rounding.
concept: Rounded quantisation error ≤ ½ LSB.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: Which rule applies to the MQTT wildcard #?
options: It matches exactly one level and may appear anywhere
It matches only the parent level and nothing below it
It matches zero or more levels and must be the last character of the filter
It must be the first character of the filter
explanation: # is a multi-level wildcard and must be last, so a/#/c is invalid, and a/# also matches a. Matching exactly one level and appearing anywhere describes +.
concept: # = zero or more levels, last only.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: Which observable MAC-layer indicators help detect jamming?
options: Topic names, QoS levels and retained flags
Channel busy ratio, number of backoffs and retransmission counts
IP address range and DNS cache size
explanation: A jammer raises the busy probability above its normal value (Δ = p_b − p_b^normal) and inflates backoffs and retries. Topic names and QoS levels are application-layer MQTT properties.
concept: Detect jamming via abnormal busy ratio, backoffs, retries.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: In ALOHA analysis, how does the offered load G differ from the throughput S?
options: G counts only new packets; S counts all attempts
G and S are always equal in steady state
G counts new plus retransmitted attempts per frame time; S counts only successful frames
G is measured in bits; S is measured in seconds
explanation: Flow balance gives G = λ + G(1 − P_s), so G exceeds the new-traffic rate by the retransmissions, while S = G·P_s equals new traffic at equilibrium. Reversing the definitions is the common error.
concept: G = all attempts; S = successful frames = λ at equilibrium.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: What is IFTTT in an IoT stack?
options: A transport protocol competing with MQTT
A MAC scheme for low-power radios
A cloud automation service whose Applets link a trigger to an action
explanation: IFTTT sits above the protocol stack: an Applet's trigger ('this'), optional filter, and action ('that') run in IFTTT's cloud. Treating it as a protocol like MQTT is the classic error.
concept: IFTTT = cloud trigger → action service, not a protocol.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: Which operations are typical of signal conditioning in a sensor chain?
options: Amplification, filtering, impedance matching and level shifting
Photon absorption in the photoconductive layer
explanation: Signal conditioning strengthens and cleans the transducer's weak output so an ADC can digitise it. Photon absorption is part of detection/transduction in an LDR, not conditioning.
concept: Signal conditioning prepares the analog signal for the ADC.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: How are responsibilities split between the LLC and MAC sublayers of the data link layer?
options: LLC handles link-level reliability (framing, sequencing, ACKs); MAC decides when a frame may enter the shared medium
LLC routes packets across hops; MAC encrypts them
LLC senses the carrier; MAC computes checksums only
LLC assigns IP addresses; MAC assigns ports
explanation: LLC gives upper layers a reliable link interface, while MAC arbitrates access to the shared channel. Routing across hops belongs to the network layer, not LLC.
concept: LLC = reliability; MAC = channel access.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: How does a passive RFID tag obtain the energy to respond to a reader?
options: It uses a small internal battery that lasts for the life of the tag
It draws power from the barcode printed beside it
It harvests energy from the electromagnetic field emitted by the reader's antenna
It is wired to the reader through a thin conductive strip
explanation: Passive tags have no battery; the reader's RF field powers the chip, which then backscatters its ID. An internal battery is the defining feature of an active tag, which is why active tags reach longer ranges.
concept: Passive tag = no battery, powered by the reader's field; active tag = own battery.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: A client subscribes to campus/B01/#. Which of these topics will it receive?
explanation: # matches zero or more levels, so it also matches the parent campus/B01. Campus/B01/F1/temp looks right but differs in case, and MQTT topics are case-sensitive.
concept: a/# also matches a.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: Using PUBLISH size = 1 + (Remaining Length bytes) + [2 + topic length + 2 (packet ID if QoS > 0) + payload], how many bytes is a QoS 1 PUBLISH to home/room1/temp with payload "28.6"?
explanation: Variable part = 2 + 15 (topic) + 2 (packet ID, since QoS 1) + 4 (payload) = 23 bytes; Remaining Length = 23 fits in 1 byte, and the control byte adds 1, giving 25. 23 bytes counts only the variable part and omits the 2-byte fixed header.
concept: MQTT fixed header ≥ 2 bytes; packet ID only when QoS > 0.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: In the ideal limit a → 0, non-persistent CSMA throughput is S = G/(1 + G). What offered load gives S = 0.9?
explanation: G/(1 + G) = 0.9 ⇒ G = 0.9/0.1 = 9. G = 0.9 assumes S equals G, which ignores idle periods in the cycle.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: 200 sensors send 10 ms packets, and the design keeps the normalised load at or below 0.1. What is the minimum reporting interval?
explanation: λT ≤ 0.1 ⇒ λ ≤ 10 packets/s, so 200 sensors may each report at most once every 20 s. A 2 s interval gives λ = 100 packets/s and λT = 1, ten times the limit.
concept: Interval ≥ N·T_pkt/G_target.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: A contaminated water valve in one building must be closed and confirmed. Which interaction fits best?
options: CoAP NON PUT with no acknowledgement
MQTT QoS 0 publish to campus/# so every device sees it
CoAP CON PUT to the valve's resource, expecting 2.04 Changed, then a GET to verify
An IFTTT applet used as the transport protocol
explanation: Directly controlling one constrained device is CoAP's strength, and CON gives an ACK while 2.04 Changed confirms the update. A NON PUT is tempting because it is lighter, but it gives no confirmation for a safety action.
concept: CoAP for direct control of one device; MQTT for fan-out telemetry.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: Slotted ALOHA: N = 5 nodes use p = 0.1, except node A, which uses 2p = 0.2. What is node A's throughput? (Round to 3 decimal places.)
explanation: S_A = 0.2 × (0.9)⁴ = 0.131, since A succeeds only if the other four stay silent. 0.066 is the symmetric per-node value before A became aggressive.
concept: Aggressive node: S_A = 2p(1 − p)^(N−1).

subject: Internet of Things
stem: Pure ALOHA runs at G = 0.5 per frame time. What is the probability that 2 or more frames start within a frame's 2T vulnerable window? (Round to 3 decimal places.)
explanation: The window holds on average 2 × 0.5 = 1 arrival, so P(≥2) = 1 − e^(−1) − e^(−1) = 0.264. 0.090 uses a window of only T.
concept: Count arrivals over the full vulnerable window.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: A 2 km cable (v = 2×10⁸ m/s) runs at 100 Mbps. What is the minimum frame length for a ≤ 0.01?
explanation: τ = 10 µs, so T ≥ τ/0.01 = 1 ms, and L = R·T = 10⁸ × 10⁻³ = 100,000 bits. 1,000 bits would give T = 10 µs and a = 1.
concept: Smaller a needs longer frames: L ≥ R·τ/a.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: 50 sensors each report once per second, and each packet occupies the channel for 10 ms. What is the normalised new-traffic load λT?
explanation: λ = 50 packets/s and λT = 50 × 0.01 = 0.5. 0.05 is the load at the slower 10 s reporting interval.
concept: Normalised load = (N/interval) × airtime.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: For N = 10 nodes using slotted ALOHA at the optimal p = 1/N, what is the maximum throughput? (Round to 3 decimal places.)
explanation: S_max = (1 − 1/N)^(N−1) = 0.9⁹ = 0.387. 0.368 is the N → ∞ limit; finite N does slightly better.
concept: Finite-N max (1 − 1/N)^(N−1) falls toward 1/e.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: An LM35 at 37.5 °C feeds a 10-bit ADC using the 1.1 V internal reference. Using the 2ⁿ − 1 convention and rounding to the nearest integer, what code is produced?
explanation: 0.375/1.1 × 1023 = 348.75, which rounds to 349. 77 is the code with a 5 V reference; the lower 1.1 V reference makes each count 4.5× finer.
concept: Lower V_ref → finer resolution, larger codes.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: Under 1-persistent CSMA, the number of stations that arrive and wait during a frame is Poisson with mean G = 2. What is the probability of a collision when the frame ends? (Round to 3 decimal places.)
explanation: All waiters send at once, so a collision occurs if 2 or more are waiting: 1 − e^(−2) − 2e^(−2) = 0.594. 0.865 is P(at least one waiter), which includes the single-waiter success case.
concept: 1-persistent: collision if ≥2 waiters at frame end.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: A sensor gives V_out = 0.375 V to a 10-bit ADC with V_ref = 5 V. Using the 2ⁿ − 1 convention and rounding to the nearest integer, what code is read?
explanation: 0.375/5 × 1023 = 76.725, which rounds to 77. 76 results from truncating rather than rounding.
concept: Round to nearest, not truncate, unless stated.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: Pure ALOHA has offered load G = 0.25. What is the throughput S? (Round to 3 decimal places.)
explanation: S = G·e^(−2G) = 0.25·e^(−0.5) = 0.152. 0.195 applies the slotted formula G·e^(−G).
concept: Pure ALOHA: S = G·e^(−2G).

subject: Internet of Things
stem: 500 sensors publish every 30 s. The number of subscribers per message rises from 4 to 100. How do the broker delivery load and publication rate change?
options: Delivery load rises 96×; publication rate halves
Delivery load rises 25×; the publication rate is unchanged
Delivery load is unchanged; publication rate rises 25×
explanation: R_del ∝ K, so 100/4 = 25×, while R_pub = N·f does not depend on K. Saying both rise confuses subscriber count with publisher activity.
concept: Broker scales with K; publishers do not.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: For pure ALOHA with N nodes, a shortcut sets p = 1/(2N) instead of the exact optimum. For N = 2, compare S = Np(1 − p)^(2(N−1)) at the exact optimum and at the shortcut. (4 dp.)
options: Both give 0.2963, because the optimum is flat
The shortcut p = 1/4 gives 0.2963, which is higher
Exact p = 1/3 gives 0.2963; the shortcut p = 1/4 gives 0.2812, a noticeable loss at small N
Exact p = 1/2 gives 0.2500, the true maximum
explanation: The exact optimum is 1/(2N − 1) = 1/3, giving 0.2963, while p = 1/4 gives 0.2812, about 5% less. Claiming the optimum is flat holds only for large N, where the two values converge.
concept: p* = 1/(2N − 1); the 1/(2N) shortcut is worst at small N.
source: Owner's IoT notes; scenario style inspired by Bahga & Madisetti, IoT: A Hands-On Approach

subject: Internet of Things
stem: An MQTT broker for a hospital-ward sensor network must be hardened. Which set of measures is most effective?
options: TLS on 8883, allow_anonymous false with per-client credentials, least-privilege ACLs, and no broad # read rights for apps
Hard-to-guess topic names on port 1883 without authentication
QoS 2 on every topic to keep data confidential
Client-side subscription filters instead of broker ACLs
explanation: Confidentiality needs TLS, identity needs authentication, and authorisation needs broker-side least-privilege ACLs. QoS 2 is tempting as 'more secure' but only governs delivery semantics, not confidentiality.
concept: Secure MQTT = TLS + authentication + least-privilege ACL.
source: Owner's IoT notes; scenario style inspired by Bahga & Madisetti, IoT: A Hands-On Approach

subject: Internet of Things
stem: A 500 m LAN with 1000-bit frames is upgraded from 10 Mbps to 1 Gbps. What happens to a = τ/T (v = 2×10⁸ m/s), and how can CSMA's efficiency be restored to a = 0.025?
options: a stays at 0.025 because distance is unchanged
a falls to 0.00025; no change is needed
a rises from 0.025 to 2.5; frames must grow to 100,000 bits
a rises to 2.5; frames must shrink to 10 bits
explanation: T falls from 100 µs to 1 µs while τ stays 2.5 µs, so a = 2.5 and CSMA degrades towards ALOHA; since a ∝ R/L, L must rise 100× to 100,000 bits. Saying a is unchanged ignores that faster bit rates shorten frame time.
concept: a ∝ R·d/L: faster links need longer frames.
source: Owner's IoT notes; scenario style inspired by Bahga & Madisetti, IoT: A Hands-On Approach

subject: Internet of Things
stem: Why do battery-powered sensor nodes usually prefer short-range radios unless wide-area coverage is essential?
options: Longer range needs more transmit energy, which shortens node lifetime
Short-range radios always provide higher security
Long-range radios cannot carry digital data
Short-range radios do not need a MAC protocol
explanation: Transmit energy grows with distance, so long-range links drain batteries faster. Short-range radios still share a medium and still need MAC, so that option is wrong.
concept: Range ↔ energy trade-off governs radio choice.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: What does MQTT QoS 1 guarantee?
options: Exactly-once delivery with a four-packet handshake
explanation: QoS 1 uses PUBLISH/PUBACK and retransmits until acknowledged, so a lost PUBACK can cause a duplicate. Exactly-once with four packets is QoS 2, and no MQTT QoS level covers deadlines.
concept: QoS 0 ≤1, QoS 1 ≥1, QoS 2 =1.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: In the six-component IoT chain, what is the correct upstream order of data flow?
options: Things → Gateway → Users → Platform → Connectivity → Applications
Things → Connectivity → Gateway → Platform → Applications → Users
Users → Applications → Platform → Gateway → Connectivity → Things
Things → Platform → Connectivity → Gateway → Applications → Users
explanation: Devices sense, connectivity carries data to a gateway, the gateway relays it to the platform, applications use it and users consume the insights. The reverse chain starting from users is the downstream control path, not the upstream data path.
concept: Upstream: things → connectivity → gateway → platform → apps → users.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: Which behaviour defines a greedy (MAC-misbehaving) node?
options: It encrypts its frames with a stronger cipher
It reports sensor readings less often
It uses a longer reporting interval to save energy
It shortens its backoff or raises its transmit probability to grab more than its fair share
explanation: Backoff manipulation violates the channel-access rules so the cheater wins contention at honest nodes' expense. Reporting less often lowers load and hurts nobody.
concept: Greedy MAC = backoff/probability manipulation for unfair share.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: After a passive RFID tag is energised, how does it send its unique ID back to the reader?
options: By modulating (backscattering) the reader's radio waves
By printing the ID as an optical pattern the reader scans
By opening a TCP connection to the cloud platform
By transmitting on its own licensed cellular channel
explanation: The tag modulates the incoming RF wave so that the reflected signal carries its UID back to the antenna. An optical pattern is how a barcode works, which needs line of sight and is exactly what RFID avoids.
concept: Passive RFID replies by backscatter modulation of the reader's signal.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: How does an LDR's resistance behave in darkness compared with bright light?
options: It is low in darkness and high in bright light
It stays constant; only its capacitance changes
It drops to zero in darkness
It is high in darkness (around 100 kΩ to 10 MΩ) and low in bright light
explanation: Without photons, few charge carriers are freed, so resistance is high; light frees carriers and resistance falls to roughly 200 Ω–10 kΩ. The reversed behaviour is the common slip, but a photoresistor conducts better when illuminated.
concept: LDR: light → low R; dark → high R.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: What is the core idea of CSMA, and when does it work well?
options: Transmit blindly and check the ACK; it works best on satellite links
Pass a token in a ring; it works best when nodes join often
Use a separate frequency per node; it works best in dense networks
Listen before talking; it works well when propagation delay is much smaller than frame time (τ ≪ T)
explanation: Sensing tells a node whether the channel is busy, but the information is only fresh if signals propagate quickly relative to frame time. Transmitting blindly is ALOHA, which is the fallback when τ is large.
concept: CSMA = sense before transmit; needs small a = τ/T.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: ALOHA was first built to connect what?
options: Universities across the mainland through leased telephone lines
Factory robots on a shared industrial bus
Satellites to ground stations using lasers
Terminals on several Hawaiian islands to a central computer over UHF radio
explanation: Undersea cables between islands were too costly, so terminals shared a radio channel to a central machine. Mainland university interconnection describes ARPANET, a different system.
concept: ALOHA: shared UHF radio linking island terminals to a central computer.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: A compromised but authenticated sensor publishes 90 °C to its usual topic. What does the broker do?
options: Rejects it because the value is out of range
Quarantines the topic until an administrator approves it
Delivers it normally; the broker cannot verify whether data is true
explanation: The broker routes and authorises by topic; it treats payloads as opaque bytes and has no notion of plausibility. Range checking must be done by subscribers or signed-data schemes, not by the broker.
concept: Broker checks access, not data truth.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: What core problem did the Internet Protocol solve?
options: Increasing the radio range of island terminals
Letting computers on different, incompatible networks communicate through one universal standard
Giving every sensor a unique RFID tag
explanation: Proliferating networks used incompatible formats, so messages could not cross between them; IP gave a single common protocol. Cheaper supercomputers was the motivation for remote-access networks like ARPANET, not for IP.
concept: IP unified incompatible networks into one internetwork.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: What is the vulnerable interval of a frame under CSMA?
explanation: Once a transmission has propagated to everyone, others sense busy and defer, so only starts within τ can collide. 2T is the pure-ALOHA vulnerable period, where no sensing is done.
concept: CSMA vulnerable window = τ.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: How can a CoAP client receive updates without polling?
options: By subscribing to a topic on a CoAP broker
By sending a DELETE to the resource
By registering with the Observe option on a GET, so the server notifies it on each change
explanation: Observe (RFC 7641) gives push-style notifications from the resource server without any broker. CoAP has no broker or QoS 2; those are MQTT concepts.
concept: CoAP Observe = server-push notifications.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: A 50-byte frame is sent at 250 kbps to a node 5 km away through air (v = 3×10⁸ m/s). What is a? (Round to 4 decimal places.)
explanation: T = 400 bits/250 kbps = 1.6 ms and τ = 16.67 µs, so a = 0.0104. 0.0833 treats 50 bytes as 50 bits, shrinking T eightfold.
concept: Convert bytes to bits before computing T.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: A jammer forces 10 retries per second, each costing 5 mJ, on a node with a 5 kJ battery. How long until half the battery is drained? (Round to 1 decimal place.)
explanation: Half the battery is 2,500 J, i.e. 2,500/0.005 = 500,000 retries, which takes 50,000 s ≈ 13.9 h at 10/s. 27.8 h is the time to drain the whole battery.
concept: Drain time = energy/(retry rate × E_retry).

subject: Internet of Things
stem: 2,000 smart meters report every 15 minutes to 5 apps; each delivered message is 80 bytes. What is the broker's outbound payload bandwidth? (Round to 1 decimal place.)
explanation: R_pub = 2000/900 = 2.22/s and R_del = 11.1/s, so 11.1 × 80 × 8 = 7.1 kbit/s. 1.4 kbit/s counts only the inbound publications, not the five-way fan-out.
concept: Bandwidth = R_del × bytes × 8.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: A campus has 5 buildings × 4 floors × 20 rooms, 3 sensors per room, each publishing every 15 s, with 2 apps subscribed to every stream. What are R_pub and R_del?
explanation: Streams = 400 rooms × 3 = 1,200, so R_pub = 1,200/15 = 80/s and R_del = 2 × 80 = 160/s. 26.67/s forgets the 3 sensors per room.
concept: Count streams first, then apply N·f and N·K·f.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: A CoAP CON message uses an initial timeout of 3 s that doubles on each retry, with MAX_RETRANSMIT = 4. If no ACK ever arrives, when is the last retransmission sent?
explanation: Transmissions occur at 0, 3, 9, 21 and 45 s (gaps 3, 6, 12, 24), so the last is at 45 s, the MAX_TRANSMIT_SPAN. 93 s is MAX_TRANSMIT_WAIT, when the sender finally gives up after the last timeout.
concept: CoAP exponential backoff: span 45 s, wait 93 s.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: In the non-persistent CSMA renewal model, packets arrive as Poisson with g = 50 per second. What is the mean idle period?
explanation: The idle period is exponential with rate g, so Ī = 1/g = 1/50 s = 20 ms. 50 ms confuses the rate with the period.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: Slotted ALOHA, N = 4, p = 0.25. What is the probability that node A's first success happens in slot 5? (Round to 4 decimal places.)
explanation: P_A = 0.25 × 0.75³ = 0.1055 per slot, so P(first success in slot 5) = (1 − P_A)⁴ P_A = 0.0675. 0.0471 uses the success probability of any node, not node A.
concept: First success in slot k: (1 − P)^(k−1)·P.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: Each attempt succeeds with P_s = 0.6 and the deadline allows 3 attempts. What is P(miss deadline), and how many attempts are needed for ε ≤ 0.05?
explanation: P_miss = (1 − 0.6)³ = 0.064 > 0.05; m ≥ ln 0.05/ln 0.4 = 3.27, so 4 attempts. 0.216 is the probability that all 3 attempts succeed, not that all fail.
concept: P_miss = (1 − P_s)^m.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: Slotted ALOHA runs at G = 0.5. What fraction of slots contain a collision? (Round to 3 decimal places.)
explanation: P(collision) = 1 − e^(−G) − G·e^(−G) = 1 − 0.607 − 0.303 = 0.090. 0.393 is P(at least one attempt), which wrongly includes successful slots.
concept: Slot outcomes: idle e^(−G), success Ge^(−G), collision remainder.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: A 12-bit ADC (V_ref = 3.3 V, 2ⁿ − 1 convention) digitises an LM35 at 37.5 °C with rounding. What are the code and the reconstructed temperature? (Temperature to 2 decimal places.)
explanation: 0.375/3.3 × 4095 = 465.34 → 465; back-converting gives 465 × 3.3/4095 = 0.37473 V → 37.47 °C, an error of about −0.03 °C. Reporting exactly 37.50 °C ignores the quantisation step.
concept: Round-trip through an ADC loses up to ½ LSB.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: On a pure-ALOHA channel, 60% of transmissions succeed. What is the offered load G? (Round to 3 decimal places.)
explanation: P_s = e^(−2G) = 0.6, so G = −ln 0.6/2 = 0.255, which is on the stable side of the 0.5 peak. 0.511 uses the slotted relation e^(−G).
concept: Invert P_s to find G: pure G = −ln P_s/2.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: ALOHA analysis models arrivals as Poisson. A switch receives 180 calls per hour on average. What is the probability of exactly 2 calls in a given minute? (Round to 3 decimal places.)
explanation: The mean per minute is L = 180/60 = 3, so P(2) = e^(−3)·3²/2! = 0.224. 0.149 is P(exactly 1); forgetting to scale k and the factorial is the usual slip.
concept: Poisson pmf: P(k) = e^(−L)·L^k/k!, with L scaled to the interval.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: Two slotted-ALOHA devices transmit with p_A = 0.3 and p_B = 0.2. What are S_A, S_B and total throughput?
explanation: S_A = p_A(1 − p_B) = 0.3 × 0.8 = 0.24 and S_B = p_B(1 − p_A) = 0.2 × 0.7 = 0.14, total 0.38. 0.21 and 0.16 multiply each node by its own idle probability instead of the other's.
concept: S_A = p_A(1 − p_B).

subject: Internet of Things
stem: An ALOHAnet packet carries 80 characters × 8 bits plus 32 header bits and 32 parity bits, and takes 29 ms to transmit. What is the channel bit rate? (Round to 2 decimal places.)
explanation: L = 640 + 32 + 32 = 704 bits, and 704/0.029 s = 24.28 kbps. 22.07 kbps counts only the payload bits.
concept: R = L/T with L including header and parity.

subject: Internet of Things
stem: Three non-persistent stations each pick a backoff uniformly from 8 slots. What is the probability that at least two pick the same slot? (Round to 3 decimal places.)
explanation: P(all distinct) = (8·7·6)/8³ = 0.656, so P(some clash) = 0.344. 0.125 is the clash probability for just two stations.
concept: Birthday-style collision: 1 − W!/((W − k)!·W^k).

subject: Internet of Things
stem: A monitoring app subscribes to # expecting to see all broker traffic, including broker statistics under $SYS/…. What does it receive?
options: Nothing, because # is invalid on its own
All normal topics but none of the $SYS/… topics; it must also subscribe to $SYS/# explicitly
explanation: Under the MQTT specification, wildcards at the first level do not match topics starting with $, so $SYS needs its own subscription. # alone is a valid filter, so 'nothing' is wrong.
concept: First-level wildcards skip $-prefixed topics.
source: Owner's IoT notes; scenario style inspired by Bahga & Madisetti, IoT: A Hands-On Approach

subject: Internet of Things
stem: 100 buildings stream water-quality telemetry to 3 apps, and operators occasionally must close one specific contaminated valve. Which architecture is best?
options: CoAP Observe from every app to every sensor, and MQTT QoS 0 for the valve
MQTT alone with QoS 2 for both, since QoS 2 guarantees the valve closes
MQTT for telemetry fan-out to the apps, and CoAP CON PUT for direct valve control with state verification
IFTTT for both telemetry and valve control, replacing all protocols
explanation: Fan-out telemetry suits broker-based pub/sub, while commanding one constrained device suits CoAP's confirmable request/response, and real systems use both. MQTT with QoS 2 alone is tempting, but QoS 2 does not confirm the actuator state.
concept: Match protocol to pattern: MQTT for fan-out, CoAP for device control.
source: Owner's IoT notes; scenario style inspired by Bahga & Madisetti, IoT: A Hands-On Approach

subject: Internet of Things
stem: Each attempt costs 1 mJ with a retry limit of 4. Normally P_s = 0.5; under jamming P_s = 0.1. Expected energy per packet is (1 − (1 − P_s)^R)/P_s mJ. Which conclusion is best supported? (2 dp energy, 1 dp delivery.)
options: Raising the retry limit is the best response, because delivery under jamming is already 93.8%
Under jamming, energy rises from 1.88 to 3.44 mJ while delivery falls from 93.8% to 34.4%, so detecting jamming and changing channel beats retrying harder
Energy is unchanged at 1.88 mJ, because the retry limit caps it
Delivery falls to 10.0% but energy falls too, so jamming saves battery
explanation: Normal: 1.875 mJ and 93.75% delivery; jammed: 3.439 mJ and 34.39%, about 1.8× the energy for roughly a third of the delivery. Raising the retry limit is tempting, but each extra attempt under jamming mostly burns energy, which is the attacker's goal.
concept: Under jamming, retries amplify energy loss; respond by detection, not persistence.
source: Owner's IoT notes; scenario style inspired by Bahga & Madisetti, IoT: A Hands-On Approach
